P3-MESH-HORIZON-SENTENCE: One difference between the mesh and the link budget has to be stated. The mesh keeps pairs of 1.0 m antennas up to 5 km apart wherever the terrain shows line of sight, although the smooth-Moon horizon of two such antennas is 3.73 km. Both are right: the ridge is not a sphere, and two antennas on two rises see each other across a valley farther than a sphere allows, while two on a plain do not. The horizon check is therefore off on the terrain mesh and on in Table 7; switched on in the mesh it would remove 6.9 % of the links between 1.0 m antennas and none between rover antennas. Under the two-ray law every link of the mesh closes 16 kbit/s at margins of 3 and 10 dB for every class; at 15 dB 94.2 % of the small rover's links and 99.1 % of the hopper's do, and in the month's trace of Section 4.2 no link in use is lost either way (Assumed on paths the terrain shows as visible: no path loss has been measured on the Moon).
P3-MESH-HOPS-SENTENCE: The median of two hops is over all 2,421 route points, each counted once. The fleet does not stand on them evenly: in the one-month trace of Section 4.2 the robots with a path to the base computer were 1.024 hops from it on average, because the work is near the base, and 5.6 % of the robot-epochs had no path at all and are in no average. Both numbers are true; the first describes the terrain and the second where this fleet works. What follows is that the one-hop condition of the link claim (Section 5.2) holds for a fleet that works within reach of the mast and not for one spread over the routes.

P3-E48-LINK-LAW-SENTENCE: The hop is 5 km long, between two antennas of the class's own height (for the base computer, the mast down to a 1.0 m robot antenna). Its loss follows the flat-ground two-ray law: free-space loss up to the breakpoint 4h<sub>1</sub>h<sub>2</sub>/λ and, beyond it, 40 log<sub>10</sub> d − 20 log<sub>10</sub>(h<sub>1</sub>h<sub>2</sub>) with the distance d and the antenna heights h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>2</sub> in metres, never less than free-space loss and independent of frequency (Derived from a direct ray and a ground-reflected ray with a reflection coefficient of −1 at grazing incidence; a NASA Johnson Space Center model of lunar surface propagation shows the same fourth-power law and its independence of frequency at long range [21]). A hop longer than the smooth-Moon horizon of its two antennas, √(2Rh<sub>1</sub>) + √(2Rh<sub>2</sub>) [63], carries nothing; for a class in that case the rate is reported at the longest hop the horizon allows. The rate is the Shannon capacity of a 1 MHz channel with 3 dBi antennas, a 5 dB noise figure and a 10 dB margin (Assumed). The rate under free-space loss at the same hop is kept beside it as an upper bound.

For the crew rover and the cargo rover the rate at that hop fell from 6,976 kbit/s to 1,574 kbit/s, and for the base mast's downlink from 9,289 kbit/s to 4,717 kbit/s.

A temperature-compensated crystal has a constant frequency error drawn per vehicle between 0 and 8 × 10<sup>−7</sup>, the range the crystal of the LuGRE receiver showed on the lunar surface as it warmed from 25 to 45 °C [82] (Measured on the Moon, read from a figure's axis). A chip-scale atomic clock has a frequency error with a standard deviation of 3 × 10<sup>−10</sup>, its temperature term, and ages by 9 × 10<sup>−10</sup> a month [86] (Spec; the data sheet says the model is not rated for space). A vehicle is synchronised by a two-way time transfer whenever it has a radio path to the base mast, which leaves a residual of 100 ns (Assumed) and corrects the offset, not the frequency (Assumed; Section 5.9 reports a variant that steers frequency). A reservation is stamped in the vehicle's own clock and keeps a guard of 0.1 s (Assumed).

The measures are the error a clock adds to one-way ranging against a beacon on the base's clock (the speed of light times the clock error), to single-sided two-way ranging between two vehicles with a reply delay of 1 ms, and to a time-stamped position at 1 m/s; the largest clock error; and the reservation conflicts caused by clock error alone. Such a conflict is a pair of conflicting single-lane reservations, of 303 such pairs in the 30 seeds, whose two clock errors close the nominal gap between them by more than twice the guard; the guard is 0.1 s, with a row for no guard. This is a check on the logged reservations, not a new run of the engine. Four things were added after the first results and are labelled post hoc (Section 4.6): guards of 0.01 and 1 s; every vehicle on Earth seconds; a transfer that also steers frequency, with a daily thermal cycle of 4 × 10<sup>−7</sup> on the crystal and 3 × 10<sup>−10</sup> on the atomic clock (Assumed period of 24 h); and a mixed fleet in which half the vehicles count Earth seconds, with and without the conversion of Proposition 3.

P3-DTN-MODEL-SENTENCE: In the model of E54 a custodian retransmits after 10 s while the link lasts and holds the bundle, in a store of 64 MB, while there is no path; a vehicle unheard for 10 min retraces its path at half speed to the last point where it had a link; and the base releases a silent vehicle's reservation 60 s after its timeout and returns its task to the auction when the 1 h lease expires (Assumed values, [68]).
P3-E54-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E54 is a simulation at the level of messages over the recorded month of E50, not a new run of the logistics engine: inside the engine a lost message is retried and the regimes know at once that it failed, so a lost job cannot occur there. The contact plan is the terrain mesh along the recorded trajectories, per 60 s step. The traffic is the month's real events: a task award from the base to each job's vehicle, which lives for the 1 h lease, and whose expiry is a lost job; a reservation grant, which lives 60 s; a task-state report at the job's end; a daily ledger bundle of 10 kB to Earth with a lifetime of 14 days; and a status report every 10 s, from which the age of the base's information is taken. Earth is blacked out from day 8 to day 22 on top of the month's own direct-to-Earth gaps. Three protocols carry the traffic: drop-and-retry end to end, a try every 180 s and at most five tries; store-and-forward hop by hop with custody; and store-and-forward with the lost-link rule of Section 3.8. The per-hop loss is 0.10, 0.25 or 0.40, on 30 seeds with 199 jobs and 88 single-lane reservations a seed. Two things are approximations: the return of a silent vehicle is applied to the contact plan and is not driven in the engine, and a returning vehicle is given a direct link to the base, which is optimistic when its last link went through another vehicle. A reservation counts as stuck when its holder has no path to the base 60 s after its timeout; under the lost-link rule the base releases it then, so the count is zero by the rule's construction, not by measurement. The ledger is simulated separately over 61 days, so that every bundle created in the month resolves, with lifetimes of 14 days, 30 days, and the longest Earth outage plus one day.
P3-E54-RESULTS-SENTENCE: At a per-hop loss of 0.25, drop-and-retry lost 10 of 6,028 task awards (4 at a loss of 0.10 and 85 at 0.40), store-and-forward with custody 2 and, with the lost-link rule, 0; the mean delay of an award was 61.5 s, 3.3 s and 3.3 s. Of the reservation grants, which live 60 s and so get one try under drop-and-retry, 1,543 were lost (25.6 %), against 2 and 0; a lost grant is a vehicle that stops before a single-lane segment. Of 6,022 task-state reports, 1,946, 82 and 2 were lost, and custody alone delivered them after 9.0 min on average, the time a report waits in a vehicle that ended its job out of reach, against 33.0 s with the lost-link rule. The base's information about a vehicle was 88.1 min old on average without the rule, and up to 30.9 h for the worst vehicle, with either transport; with the rule it was 45.5 s and 2.5 min. P3-E55-AUTH-SENTENCE: The acceptance of forged messages was measured with the real AES-CMAC truncated to a short code, because the 8-byte code cannot be tried often enough: 395 of 100,000 forged messages passed a code truncated to 8 bits, where 2<sup>−8</sup> predicts 391; 11 of 1,000,000 forged messages passed a code truncated to 16 bits, where 2<sup>−16</sup> predicts 15.3. For the 64-bit code of the narrow channel the same law gives 5.4 × 10<sup>−20</sup> per attempt and 1.7 × 10<sup>−11</sup> for ten attempts a second over a year (formula, not a trial). Of 1,172 recorded messages replayed after 0 to 60 s to receivers that keep the per-sender counter and the 10 s freshness window, 574 at a loss of 0.10 and 598 at a loss of 0.25, none was accepted. The one replay the rule admits is to a receiver that missed the original and gets the copy within the window: it then learns a true but stale state.

On the terrain mesh that held in 10 % to 26 % of the draws at fleet positions and in 0 % of the draws spread over the routes, so the rule needs more links, relays or masts, or the base as the averaging node. The pre-registered test of the rule, H16 of [67], is not supported as stated, and the companion paper reports it [61].

P3-B97-DESIGN-SENTENCE: Two checks use real data, and each is named for what it is. The first takes six raw frames of the optical-navigation camera of the Artemis II flyby, taken between 2 April 2026 and 10 April 2026 [115], fits a circle to the bright limb of the disc in each (a threshold, a robust circle fit, a least-squares refinement), and turns the disc's radius and centre into a range and a direction with the focal length of the mission's instrument kernel, 7,312 pixels; the truth is the mission's own trajectory and attitude kernels [116]. Nothing is calibrated, and the body in view is taken from the geometry, not from the archive label. This is limb navigation of a crewed spacecraft in cislunar space, 79,000 to 186,000 km from the body in view; it is not surface navigation and not rover data. It tests the camera model, the frames and the kernels that position-from-image code rests on. The second check compares the Earth-link geometry code of [58], which the Earth windows of this paper come from, with the SPICE toolkit's own routine for azimuth and elevation, for the spacecraft seen from the base at 212 hourly epochs of its trajectory, and measures how far the base moves when the lunar frame kernel is left out (Section 3.7).
P3-B97-RESULTS-SENTENCE: Artemis II optical navigation: of the six frames, one is saturated and five usable; four of those have attitude data and one gives a range only. The range from the fitted disc was 0.25 % to 1.29 % above the kernels' range, and the direction within 0.08° to 0.16°. The errors are not random: the fitted radius was 0.8 to 1.3 pixels small in every frame, which puts every range high, and the angle off the camera's axis was 0.08° to 0.11° low in every frame, which may be the alignment of the camera frame (the mission's frame kernel carries a warning about those angles). We report the bias as it is and do not fit it away; a correction fitted on other frames is the next check. Two of the five discs are Earth, although every archive label names the Moon. For the two frames of the Moon at about 79,000 km the error is 408 to 661 km in range and, at the direction errors above, about 110 to 230 km across the line of sight. That says the geometry chain recovers a real body's range to about a percent and its direction to a tenth or two of a degree from one uncalibrated frame. It says nothing about the 1.7 m of a rover's terrain fix (Table 4): that matches craters metres away against a map, a different measurement at a different scale. Earth-link geometry: over 212 epochs the code agreed with the toolkit's routine to 6 × 10<sup>−14</sup>°; without the lunar frame kernel the base moved by 77.4 m, the silent error of Section 3.7 measured at our site.

P3-P6-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: Under the market, ranging keeps position within the 5 m budget near the base (4.2 m) but terrain fixes do not away from it (15.2 m); a crystal clock suffices for reservations, not ranging; authentication adds 52 % to the bit rate.
P3-P6-INTRO-CLAUSE: Of the layers under the market, with the hypotheses of [67]: dead reckoning alone passes the 5 m separation budget within the first driving hour and ranging holds 4.22 m at the 95th percentile near the base (H9's first two clauses, supported), while terrain fixes leave 15.2 m away from the base, and 7.54 m even with a navigation service as assumed for 2030 (third clause, not supported). A crystal oscillator resynchronised whenever the base is heard causes no reservation conflict with a guard of 0.1 s, although its error adds 975 km or more to one-way ranging (H11, supported). After a day out of contact a hazards-first sync brings a rover's map up to date with 1.06 % of a full resend (H12, supported). Authentication adds 52 % to the bit rate, and 20 rovers still load the busiest link with 7.86 kbit/s at 1 Hz (H13, supported). Store-and-forward with a lost-link rule lost no job where drop-and-retry lost 0.33 a seed (H14, supported). A ledger bundle that lives 14 days does not outlast an Earth outage of 24.8 days, and 35 % of the month's ledger was lost with store-and-forward, none with a lifetime of 25.8 days.
P3-P6-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: Near the base, in view of the beacons, ranging holds the 95th percentile of the position error at 4.22 m, inside the 5 m budget; a crystal resynchronised at every contact causes no reservation conflict with a guard of 0.1 s; a day of map changes is 1.97 MB; and the authenticated reports of 20 rovers need 9.82 kbit/s of a scheduled channel. Away from the base, terrain fixes leave the 95th percentile at 15.2 m (7.54 m with a navigation service as assumed for 2030, still outside the budget), and of 20 rovers spread over the routes only 62 % reach the base at all.
P3-P6-CONCLUSION-CLAUSE: Under the market, ranging holds the 5 m position budget near the base but terrain fixes do not away from it; authentication adds 52 % to the bit rate.
